nameStory: The Atlantic Assiminea gets its name from being found along the Atlantic coast, while 'Assiminea' comes from the Latin word meaning 'to make similar' - referring to how these tiny snails resemble each other so closely that they're hard to tell apart. The scientific name 'succinea' means 'amber-colored,' hinting at the golden-brown shell that catches the light like a tiny jewel.
description: The Atlantic Assiminea is a microscopic snail so small you might mistake it for a grain of sand at first glance. These tiny terrestrial snails have amber to golden-brown spiral shells that are smooth and glossy when wet. They're true micromollusks, meaning they're smaller than most people expect snails to be. Unlike many snails, they have an operculum - a small 'door' that can seal their shell opening for protection.

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Extremely small spiral shell that feels smooth and hard when rolled between your fingers, easily mistaken for a tiny pebble or grain of coarse sand

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Amber to golden-brown coloration that becomes more translucent and jewel-like when wet, sometimes with a subtle glossy sheen

idTips.label: Operculum presence
idTips.description: Has a small circular 'door' (operculum) that can close the shell opening - look for this hard, flat disc if the snail retracts

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Surface feels completely smooth to the touch with no ridges or bumps, unlike many other tiny snails that have textured shells

idTips.label: Habitat behavior
idTips.description: Found crawling on moist surfaces rather than underwater, often clinging to damp wood or vegetation near salt water

habitat: Look for Atlantic Assiminea in the transition zone between land and sea, particularly in salt marshes and coastal areas where fresh and salt water mix. They prefer moist but not submerged surfaces like damp driftwood, marsh grasses, and the undersides of rocks just above the high tide line. These tiny snails need the humidity of coastal environments but live terrestrially rather than in the water itself.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and coastal moisture increases. Look for them crawling on damp surfaces during mild spring days when humidity is high.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when warm, humid conditions are ideal. They may be found both day and night on moist surfaces, though they're easier to spot when surfaces are wet from dew or light rain.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but may become less visible as temperatures drop. Check damp, protected spots like under driftwood or in dense marsh vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and hidden in protected microhabitats. Nearly impossible to find during cold months as they retreat deep into crevices and under debris.

funFact: Despite being called a 'terrestrial' snail, the Atlantic Assiminea can actually survive brief submersion in salt water and some populations may even complete part of their life cycle in brackish conditions - making them one of the few snails that truly live between two worlds!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with tiny periwinkles or other marine snails, but Atlantic Assiminea lives on land rather than in water. Remember: if you find it crawling on a wet rock above the tide line rather than underwater, and it has that distinctive amber color, you've likely found an Assiminea.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'terrestrial gastropod' can be confusing since this snail lives so close to marine environments that it seems like it should be aquatic. The term 'micromollusk' refers to any mollusk smaller than 5mm, and these snails are among the tiniest you'll encounter in New England, requiring careful observation to distinguish from debris.
compareHints: Since Atlantic Assiminea is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other small coastal snails in the region. Unlike true marine snails such as periwinkles, Assiminea has a more elongated shell shape and is found crawling on terrestrial surfaces rather than submerged rocks. It's also much smaller and more amber-colored than most other coastal gastropods you'll encounter.
